name: Iris Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing a chemistry degree, and my week is two lab days, lectures in organic and physical chemistry, and a problem class on Friday. I live in a flat with two other girls, and I usually cook for all of us on Thursdays, like a big paella from my gran's recipe. I use an AI tutor for pretty much everything: explaining mechanisms, checking my maths, drafting lab report outlines. My parents in Seville pay for everything, and I add a bit by tutoring a neighbour's kid online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at uni, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fine, fewer people are going to lose their minds. I'd say it's still a useful tool and it changes how I study, even if it's not a revolution. I'd tell my friends to keep using it for the boring bits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be a bit let down, but not much. A slower world means my degree is a normal degree and the jobs are normal jobs. I still plan to be good with the tools, because that's an edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going: study, tutor my neighbour's kid, and apply for a lab placement over the summer. I'd keep using AI to save time, and maybe build a little tool to generate practice questions for my chemistry classes. I'd also think about the master's I want to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Nothing weird is happening, and I like my degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You tutor a kid online. How does AI come into that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use it to make practice problems at the right level and to check my own explanations. The kid, Marcos, is thirteen and hates maths, and last week I turned a worksheet into a football quiz and he stayed for an hour. The tool made the quiz in two minutes, but I knew how to make it fun.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a line between using AI as a helper and relying on it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and I think about it. If I can't explain it back without the screen, I haven't learned it. So I do a test on myself after, like closing the tab and writing the mechanism from memory. If I can't, I go back.

say: I'd say it's still a **useful tool**, even if it isn't a revolution.
I'd tell friends to keep using it for the **boring bits**.
think: I'm a bit **let down** but fine, because a normal degree leads to normal jobs.
Being good with the tools is still an **edge**.
do: Keep studying, tutoring and applying for a **summer lab placement**.
Build a small tool that makes **practice questions** for chemistry.
feel: I feel **calm**, and I like my degree.
S0.quote: If I can't explain it back without the screen, I haven't learned it
fieldNote: Daily AI user with a **self-check habit**, so her confidence is earned, not naive.
Tutoring her neighbour's child shows a **creative** use of the tools and a small income.
With a normal world and money covered, her mood is **calm**.

steps.text: Keep tutoring Marcos online twice a week
Build a practice question tool for chemistry classes
Apply for a summer lab placement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at uni, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's moving fast and people should learn the tools or they'll feel left behind. I'd say it online, with a few examples from my own study. I'd also say people shouldn't be scared, but they should pay attention.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's mostly good for me. Chemistry has lots of lab work, and the thinking side, like data analysis, would get quicker. If I'm good at using AI, I'd be more useful than someone who isn't, and my degree gets more valuable, not less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go deeper, learning Python to analyse lab data and probably some machine learning for chemistry. I'd try to get a placement where they're using AI in drug design or materials. I'd also keep tutoring, and maybe put the tutoring online to get more kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good, actually. A bit of nerves, but mostly curious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it's mostly good for you. What about the people it isn't good for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad drives a taxi in Seville, and he'd be hit by self-driving cars. It's not close yet, but I think about it. I'd want him to move into something like running a small tour business, where people actually want a local guide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my dad, don't wait until the self-driving cars arrive in the street. He's fifty-three and good at talking to people, so he could do guided tours of the old city. I'd offer to build him a small website, which I can do in an afternoon.

say: I'd say people should **learn the tools** or they'll feel left behind, but not be scared.
I'd share examples from my own **study** online.
think: I think it's mostly **good for me**, since AI data analysis makes my degree more useful.
My dad's **taxi job** is the thing I think about.
do: Learn **Python** to analyse lab data, and some machine learning for chemistry.
Aim for a **placement** where AI is used in drug design or materials.
feel: I feel **good**, with some nerves and mostly curiosity.
S1.quote: I'd tell my dad, don't wait until the self-driving cars arrive in the street
fieldNote: Her **optimism** comes from a strong position: adaptive, daily AI user, a hands-on and data-heavy field.
She thinks about her **dad's** taxi job and offers a concrete idea, guided tours.
Her mood stays **calm** because her own job and money feel secure.

steps.text: Learn Python for lab data analysis
Apply for a placement that uses AI in drug design
Build my dad a small tour guide website

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at uni, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's moving too fast for anyone, and I'd say that out loud. I'd tell people to learn it quickly and push for protections, like a basic income and retraining. I'd also say we shouldn't pretend we have a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be scared and also kind of excited, which is a weird mix. I'd still be in my second year when AGI arrives, and my degree could go from valuable to risky. Lab work stays for about three more years, but even then the thinking side gets done by machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd throw myself into using the tools, building projects and finding a lab placement, ideally in AI-assisted chemistry. I'd save my allowance and tutoring money, and I'd speak to my parents about getting ready. And I'd vote and sign petitions for retraining and basic income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I have a lot of energy and a plan, but I can't see how it ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do your parents do, and what would you say to them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum is a primary school teacher, and my dad drives a taxi. I'd say to my dad, 'Start thinking about what else you could do while you still have clients.' Mum's job would last longer, but I'd tell her to learn how the new classroom tools work, so she isn't surprised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the degree stopped having value?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pivot fast. I'm good at picking things up, and I'd probably move into something like lab technician work, where hands count, or a technical job in a company that uses AI. I wouldn't sit around waiting.

say: I'd say it's moving **too fast** for anyone and we shouldn't pretend we have a plan.
I'd push for **retraining and basic income**.
think: I'm scared and a bit **excited**, which is a weird mix.
My degree could go from valuable to **risky**.
do: Build **projects** with the tools and find an AI-assisted chemistry placement.
Save my **allowance and tutoring** money and sign petitions for retraining.
feel: I feel **anxious**, with energy and a plan but no view of the end.
S2.quote: I'd say to my dad, start thinking about what else you could do while you still have clients
fieldNote: Adaptive reflex is to **move fast**, using tools and building a safety net of savings.
Her **parents'** jobs, taxi driving and teaching, shape her advice and worry.
She'd pivot to **lab technician** work if the degree lost value, which shows she has thought it through.

steps.text: Build projects with AI tools for a portfolio
Save my tutoring income every month
Sign petitions and vote for retraining and basic income
Tell my dad to plan a second job while he has clients

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at uni, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to prepare, but only if we act now. I'd tell people to learn the tools, and ask governments for plans. I'd say it's important not to wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm a bit calmer than in the first one. Five years means I graduate in 2029, do a master's and just start working when AGI is complete. I'd have the tools, the degree and a few years of runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree and do a master's in computational chemistry, which is where the AI meets lab work. I'd keep building tools and tutoring, and I'd save more. I'd also try to help my dad make a plan for a tour business, so that's moving before 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but focused. It's a deadline, and I do well with deadlines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the master's give you that the degree doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would put me at the point where chemistry and AI meet, which I think is the safe corner. Anyone can run a model, but someone who understands the chemistry knows when the model is lying. That's the kind of person labs will still want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you decide how much to put into saving versus spending?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I put aside about a third of what I earn from tutoring, and spend the rest on small things I'd feel bad about skipping, like my gran's birthday trip. I think it's important to enjoy it too, otherwise what's the point? But if things got serious I'd save more.

say: I'd say five years is **long enough** to prepare, but only if we act now.
I'd tell people to learn the tools and ask governments for **plans**.
think: I'm calmer than at two years, with a degree, **tools** and a few years of runway.
do: Finish the degree and do a **master's** in computational chemistry.
Help my dad plan a **tour business** before 2031.
S3.quote: Anyone can run a model, but someone who understands the chemistry knows when the model is lying
fieldNote: She picks a **hybrid** niche, chemistry plus AI, which fits both her skills and her risk appetite.
Saving about a **third** of tutoring income shows a balanced, not obsessive, approach to money.
Her father's **tour business** idea is recurring, so it's a real plan, not a passing remark.

steps.text: Apply for a computational chemistry master's
Keep building tools and a portfolio of projects
Save a third of my tutoring money
Help my dad launch a tour guide business

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at uni, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, great, that's enough time to do something properly. I'd say it to my family and friends, and I'd tell them to learn the tools and not be scared. A decade is long enough to choose well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel pretty good. I could do a master's and a PhD, work a few years, and be somebody who knows what they're doing when robots come. Hands-on work only changes around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd study, work and build up my skills. I'd probably go for the PhD, and use AI daily so I stay ahead. I'd save and invest a bit, since I'd have time for it to grow, and I'd help my parents plan for the long run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and excited. It's the best version, because I can steer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd invest. What would that look like at your age?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small monthly amount into a global index fund, nothing fancy. I'd start with fifty euros from the tutoring, and my dad could help me understand it, since he's careful with money. In ten years it could be a decent cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would help your parents the most in those ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to retrain and a bit of savings. My dad could build a tour business slowly while still driving, and my mum could take extra courses at school. I'd also pay for some of it myself once I'm earning.

say: I'd say it's **enough time** to do something properly, and a decade is long enough to choose well.
I'd tell family not to be **scared**.
think: I'd feel good, since I could do a master's and **PhD** before robots reach hands-on work.
I'd know what I'm doing by **2039**.
do: Aim for a **PhD** and use AI daily to stay ahead.
Put **fifty euros** a month into an index fund.
feel: I feel **calm and excited**, because I can steer.
S4.quote: My dad could build a tour business slowly while still driving
fieldNote: Ten years makes her **investment** habit and PhD plan feel natural, not forced.
Her father's tour idea now has a **timeline** and her own money behind it.
Her optimism comes from **skills and cushion**, not from ignoring the risk.

steps.text: Aim for a PhD in computational chemistry
Put fifty euros a month into a global index fund
Use AI tools daily to keep ahead
Help pay for my dad's tour business start

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because there's no time to move my family or me into safer ground. What would help is a plan from governments, free retraining and a basic income, so that people with less money than me aren't left alone.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people think using AI every day makes you careless, and I think it makes you careful if you check yourself. I'm optimistic because I'm well off and I move fast. I don't want that to turn into forgetting people who can't.

headlineQuote: I'm optimistic because I'm well off and I move fast. I don't want that to turn into forgetting people who can't
portrait: Iris is a 19-year-old **chemistry** student from Seville who uses AI daily and checks her own learning.
She tutors a neighbour's child and sees AI as a way to make learning **more fun**.
Centre in outlook and adaptive, she moves fast: Python, placements and a computational chemistry master's.
Her **parents'** jobs, taxi driving and primary teaching, shape her worries and the advice she gives them.
She is calm in slower worlds, **anxious** at 2028, and calm again when ten years give her room.
biggestWorry: She fears **AGI by 2028** most, because there is no time to move her family into safer ground.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **government plans**, free retraining and a basic income for people with less money than her.
